title: Poutine with oven-baked fries

ingredients.note: floury, such as russet or Maris Piper, cut into 1 cm sticks

steps: Soak the potato sticks in cold water for 30 minutes, drain and dry thoroughly. Heat the oven to 230 C.

Toss the fries with the oil and salt, spread on two trays in a single layer and bake 35 to 40 minutes, turning once, until crisp and golden. Deep-frying at 180 C for 4 to 5 minutes, twice, gives a more classic result.
For the gravy, melt the butter in a saucepan, stir in the flour and cook for 3 minutes until nutty and pale brown.
Whisk in the hot stock gradually, bring to a simmer and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until thick enough to coat a spoon. Season with pepper and salt.
Pile the hot fries into bowls, scatter the cheese curds over, and pour the boiling-hot gravy on top so the curds begin to soften. Eat immediately.
notes: Curds should be fresh and mild, and squeak when bitten. Mozzarella chunks are a poor substitute but can work.

title: Quebec pork tourtière
steps: Make the pastry: rub the butter into the flour and 1 tsp salt until it looks like breadcrumbs, add the water and bring together into two discs, one slightly larger. Chill for 1 hour.
For the filling, cook the pork, onion and garlic in a pan over medium heat, breaking up the meat, for 10 minutes.
Add the stock and spices and simmer for 20 minutes until most of the liquid is absorbed. Stir in the mashed potato to bind, season well, and cool completely.
Heat the oven to 200 C. Roll out the larger disc to line a 23 cm pie dish. Fill with the cooled meat.
Roll out the second disc, cover the pie, trim and crimp the edges, cut steam vents, and brush with beaten egg.
Bake for 15 minutes, then lower to 180 C and bake for 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden. Rest 15 minutes before cutting.
notes: Many families use a mix of pork and veal or beef. It is often served with ketchup or fruit chutney.

title: Maple taffy on snow
steps: Fill a large tray or pan with clean, packed snow or finely crushed ice and keep it outside or in the freezer.
Boil the syrup in a deep, heavy pan over medium-high heat. It will foam up, so use a pan at least four times its volume.
Heat to 112 to 115 C on a candy thermometer, which takes about 12 to 15 minutes.
Remove from the heat and let the bubbles settle for a moment.
Pour the syrup in thin ribbons onto the snow. After a few seconds, when it has set to a chewy taffy, roll it onto a wooden stick or fork.
Eat right away. Repeat while the syrup is still pourable; reheat gently if it thickens.
notes: Beware of burns from boiling syrup. Do not use flavoured table syrup, which will not set.

title: Maple pouding chômeur
steps: Heat the oven to 180 C and butter a 20 cm square baking dish.
Cream the butter and sugar, beat in the egg, then fold in the flour mixed with the baking powder, alternating with the milk, until a thick batter forms.
Spread the batter in the dish.
Heat the maple syrup, cream and salt together until just simmering, then pour it slowly over the batter. Do not stir.
Bake for 30 to 35 minutes until the cake is golden and risen and the sauce is bubbling around it.
Rest for 10 minutes and serve warm, spooned with plenty of sauce.
notes: Use a dish with sides at least 5 cm high so the syrup does not overflow.

title: Home-cured smoked meat

ingredients.note: brisket flat, with some fat left on
curing salt #1 (pink salt, sodium nitrite), measured exactly

steps: Heat the water with the salt, sugar, curing salt and garlic until dissolved, then chill completely.
Submerge the brisket in the cold brine in a non-reactive container, weighting it down, and refrigerate for 6 to 7 days, turning once every day or two.
Rinse the meat and soak it in cold water for 1 hour. Pat dry.
Mix the coriander, pepper and mustard seed and press them thickly over the surface of the meat.
Smoke at about 120 C over hardwood for about 4 hours to an internal temperature of 85 C. In an oven, bake at 120 C on a rack for 4 hours with a pan of water; smoke flavour will be lighter.
Wrap tightly in foil and steam or cook in a low oven at 110 C for 2 more hours, until a probe slides in easily at about 93 C.
Rest for 20 minutes and cut thickly against the grain. Serve on rye bread with yellow mustard and a dill pickle.
notes: Curing salt is toxic in large amounts, so use exactly the quantity given and keep it out of reach of children. Leftovers keep a week refrigerated and reheat well by steaming.

title: Newfoundland Jiggs dinner

ingredients.note: salted beef brisket or navel, soaked in cold water overnight with two changes
yellow, soaked overnight, for the pease pudding
for mashing the turnip and peas; omit to keep the dish dairy-free

steps: Drain the soaked beef, put it in a large pot with fresh cold water to cover, and bring to a boil. Skim the foam, lower the heat and simmer for 1.5 hours.
Drain the split peas, tie them loosely in a clean cloth or a muslin bag with room to swell, and add to the pot. Simmer for another 1 hour.
Add the carrots and turnip to the pot and cook for 20 minutes, then add the potatoes for 20 minutes more.
Add the cabbage wedges for the final 15 minutes until just tender.
Lift out the beef, wrap in foil to rest. Remove the pease pudding, open the cloth, and mash the peas with the butter, pepper and a little cooking liquid.
Mash the turnip with a little butter if you like. Slice the beef and serve with all the vegetables, the pease pudding and some of the cooking liquid as gravy.
notes: Salt beef is salty; taste the cooking liquid and change the water if it is too strong. It is sold in some butchers and Atlantic Canadian markets, or you can use home-cured or corned brisket.

title: Ontario butter tarts
steps: Rub the cold butter into the flour and a pinch of salt until crumbly, add the water and press into a dough. Chill for 1 hour.
Heat the oven to 200 C. Roll the pastry 3 mm thick and cut twelve 10 cm rounds. Press them into a 12-hole muffin tin.
Whisk the melted butter with the sugar, maple syrup, egg, vinegar and salt until smooth.
If using raisins, put a few in each shell. Spoon the filling in, filling each case about two-thirds so that it will not overflow.
Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until the pastry is golden and the filling bubbles.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then loosen with a knife and lift out to a rack. The filling thickens as it cools.
notes: For a runnier filling reduce baking time slightly, for a firmer one bake until the centres no longer wobble.

title: Potato and cheddar pyrohy
steps: Mix the flour with 1 tsp salt, the egg, sour cream and water, then knead for 5 minutes into a soft, smooth dough. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
Fry the chopped onion in 15 g of the butter until golden. Mash the potatoes, add the onion and cheddar, and season with salt and a good amount of pepper. Cool.
Roll the dough 2 mm thick and cut 8 cm circles. Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the middle of each, fold over, and pinch the edges tightly to seal.
Cook in batches in simmering salted water for 3 to 4 minutes after they float.
Melt the rest of the butter in a pan and fry the sliced onions until golden. Add the boiled pyrohy and fry briefly until lightly browned.
Serve with the onions and sour cream.
notes: Uncooked pyrohy freeze well on a tray and can be boiled from frozen, adding 2 minutes. Cottage cheese or sauerkraut are other classic fillings.

title: Pan-fried bannock

ingredients.note: plus extra for the pan; lard is traditional

steps: Stir the flour, baking powder and salt together in a bowl.
Rub or stir in the 3 tbsp oil, then add the water gradually and mix lightly to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Do not overwork.
Pat the dough out to a disc about 2 cm thick, or divide into six smaller rounds.
Heat a heavy frying pan over medium-low heat with a thin film of oil. Fry the bannock for 8 to 10 minutes on each side, turning once, until golden and cooked through, with a hollow sound when tapped.
Serve warm, split, with soup, stew, jam or butter.
notes: Cooking over a low heat matters, otherwise the outside burns before the middle cooks. It can also be baked at 200 C for 20 to 25 minutes. Dried berries are a common addition.

title: Classic Nanaimo bars
steps: Line a 20 cm square tin with baking paper.

For the base, melt the first measure of butter with the sugar and cocoa in a heatproof bowl over simmering water. Stir in the egg and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens like custard. Do not let the egg scramble.
Remove from the heat, stir in the crumbs, coconut and almonds. Press firmly into the tin and chill for 20 minutes.
Beat the softened butter, milk, custard powder and icing sugar for the middle layer until smooth and fluffy. Spread over the chilled base and chill another 20 minutes.
Melt the chocolate with the tablespoon of butter, cool slightly and spread evenly over the middle layer.
Chill for 2 hours, or until the chocolate is just set. Cut into squares with a hot knife, cleaning it between cuts.
notes: The egg in the base is cooked gently in the custard step. Keep the bars refrigerated and eat within 5 days. Walnuts are sometimes used in place of almonds.
